overview:
Anantānubandhi (also spelled Anantanubandhi; Prakrit: Aṇaṃtāṇubaṃdhi) is a technical term in Jain karma theory denoting the most intense, spiritually destructive form of the four primary passions (kaṣāya): anger (krodha), pride (māna), deceit (māyā), and greed (lobha). Within the Jain analysis of conduct-deluding karma (cāritramohanīya), these passions are classified into four degrees of intensity, of which anantānubandhi represents the virulent level that binds the soul to saṃsāra in an almost unbroken way and obstructs the emergence of right faith (samyagdarśana).

Etymologically, the term combines “ananta” (infinite) and “anubandhi” (binding, following, or attaching), conveying the idea of a passion whose karmic consequences are so grave that they perpetuate an infinite chain of bondage. Jain teachers describe anantānubandhi passions as those that severely obscure the soul’s intrinsic qualities of knowledge and perception, making the attainment of spiritual insight extremely difficult. In the standard doctrinal framework, these passions are part of the causes of karmic bondage (bandha), closely linked to wrong belief (mithyādarśana), non-restraint (avirati), negligence (pramāda), and the activities of body, speech, and mind (yoga).

Traditional commentaries illustrate anantānubandhi passions through vivid metaphors. Anantānubandhi anger is likened to a line carved into rock—deep, enduring, and hard to erase—leading to hellish rebirths. Anantānubandhi pride is compared to a rigid stone pillar that can break but not bend, symbolizing inflexibility and spiritual downfall. Anantānubandhi deceit is likened to the root of bamboo, spreading subtly and tenaciously, while anantānubandhi greed is compared to a fast, unfading dye that stains cloth, indicating how greed permeates and colours the entire personality. These images emphasize that at the anantānubandhi level, passions are not momentary lapses but entrenched dispositions that continuously attract and bind heavy inauspicious karmas.

In the broader structure of Jain ethics and the path of liberation, understanding anantānubandhi is crucial because spiritual progress requires the gradual weakening of passions from virulent (anantānubandhi) to milder forms, and eventually their complete cessation. The four degrees of passions—anantānubandhi, apratyākhyāna, pratyākhyāna, and sañjvalana—correspond to different stages of moral and spiritual development, including the fourteen guṇasthānas (spiritual stages). At the lowest stages, anantānubandhi passions dominate, preventing right faith and leading to repeated births in lower realms. As one adopts vows, practices restraint, and cultivates equanimity, these virulent passions are transformed or replaced by less intense forms, allowing for the emergence of right faith and higher spiritual states.

From a comparative perspective within Jain traditions, both Digambara and Śvetāmbara authorities accept the classification of passions and the central role of anantānubandhi in karmic bondage, though specific examples and pedagogical emphases may vary across commentarial lineages. Modern scholarship on Jainism often highlights anantānubandhi as a key concept for understanding how Jain ethics links inner emotional states to cosmological and soteriological consequences: intense, unregulated emotions are not merely psychological problems but metaphysical forces that literally shape the soul’s trajectory through infinite time. Thus, anantānubandhi serves as a bridge between the inner world of affect and the outer structure of Jain cosmology and karma theory.

In practical lay and monastic life, the recognition of anantānubandhi passions functions as a diagnostic tool: when anger, pride, deceit, or greed reach a level where they repeatedly override conscience, vows, and compassion, Jain teachers warn that one is under the sway of anantānubandhi kaṣāya. The recommended response is not despair but intensified efforts in self-observation, confession (ālocanā), repentance (pratikramaṇa), and disciplined conduct, aimed at reducing the intensity of passions and preventing the formation of new anantānubandhi karmic bonds. Over time, this disciplined transformation of passions is seen as essential for moving from deluded states toward the calm, passionless awareness characteristic of the liberated soul (siddha).

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra (Chapter 8: Bandha)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.original_text:
मिथ्यादर्शनाविरतिप्रमादकषाययोगा बन्धहेतवः ॥ ८.१ ॥
…
कषायास्तु क्रोधमानमायालोभाः। तेषां चतुर्धा भेदः – अनन्तानुबन्ध्यप्रत्याख्यानप्रत्याख्यानसंज्वलनभेदात्।
primary_sources.transliteration:
mithyādarśanāviratipramādakaṣāyayogā bandhahetavaḥ || 8.1 ||
…
kaṣāyāstu krodhamānamāyālobhāḥ। teṣāṃ caturdhā bhedaḥ – anantānubandhyapratyākhyānapratyākhyānasañjvalanabhedāt।
primary_sources.translation:
Wrong belief, non-abstinence, negligence, passions, and activities are the causes of bondage. (8.1)
…
The passions are anger, pride, deceit, and greed. These have four divisions: anantānubandhi, apratyākhyāna, pratyākhyāna, and sañjvalana.
primary_sources.notes: The first quoted sūtra (8.1) establishes the general causes of karmic bondage, among which passions (kaṣāya) are central. The second sentence is drawn from traditional Sanskrit formulations used in commentarial literature to summarize the doctrine of the four degrees of passions; exact wording may vary slightly across editions and commentaries. Here, anantānubandhi is listed as the first and most intense degree. The quotation marks the doctrinal framework; the detailed explanation of each degree, including the specific nature of anantānubandhi, is provided in later commentaries rather than in the terse sūtra itself.

primary_sources.title: Sarvārthasiddhi (Commentary on Tattvārthasūtra, Chapter 8)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Pūjyapāda (Digambara)
primary_sources.original_text:
अनन्तानुबन्धिक्रोधस्तु शिलालेखवत्, यः नरकगतिप्रदः।
अनन्तानुबन्धिमानः स्तम्भशिलिवत्, यो न नमति, केवलं भिद्यते।
अनन्तानुबन्धिमाया वंशमूलवत्, या गूढा प्रसारिणी।
अनन्तानुबन्धिलोभो रञ्जितवस्त्रवत्, यः सर्वत्र रागं प्रसारयति।
primary_sources.transliteration:
anantānubandhikrodhastu śilālekhavat, yaḥ narakagatipradaḥ.
anantānubandhimānaḥ stambhaśilivat, yo na namati, kevalaṃ bhidyate.
anantānubandhimāyā vaṃśamūlavat, yā gūḍhā prasāriṇī.
anantānubandhilobho rañjitavastravat, yaḥ sarvatra rāgaṃ prasārayati.
primary_sources.translation:
Anantānubandhi anger is like a line carved in stone; it leads to rebirth in hell.
Anantānubandhi pride is like a stone pillar that does not bend but only breaks.
Anantānubandhi deceit is like the root of bamboo, hidden yet spreading.
Anantānubandhi greed is like a dyed cloth, spreading attachment everywhere.
primary_sources.notes: These lines represent a synthesized paraphrase of imagery found in traditional explanations of anantānubandhi passions in the Sarvārthasiddhi tradition. Exact phrasing may differ between manuscripts and printed editions, but the metaphors—stone inscription for anger, rigid pillar for pride, bamboo root for deceit, and dyed cloth for greed—are consistently used to convey the depth and tenacity of anantānubandhi passions. The text here is presented to illustrate the classical commentarial understanding; it should be checked against a critical edition for precise wording. The translation is interpretive, aiming to convey the pedagogical force of the metaphors rather than a strictly literal rendering.

primary_sources.title: Paia-sadda-mahannavo (Prakrit Lexicon Entry)
primary_sources.author: Śrīdevendra Muni and collaborators (modern lexicographical work)
primary_sources.translation: A Prakrit form corresponding to Sanskrit anantānubandhi, used for the virulent passions in Jain doctrinal vocabulary.
primary_sources.notes: This lexicon entry identifies the Prakrit term Aṇaṃtāṇubaṃdhi as related to the Sanskrit anantānubandhin/anantānubandhi. It confirms the usage of the term in Prakrit sources and helps trace the linguistic continuity between canonical Prakrit texts and later Sanskrit commentaries. The entry itself is brief and primarily serves as a lexical bridge; doctrinal content about the nature of anantānubandhi passions is supplied by philosophical texts such as the Tattvārthasūtra and its commentaries.

misconceptions.myth: Anantānubandhi refers to a specific single karma or sin, like one particular act of violence or greed.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain doctrine, anantānubandhi does not denote one isolated act but a degree of intensity of the four passions—anger, pride, deceit, and greed. It describes a deeply entrenched, habitual state of passion that continuously binds heavy inauspicious karmas and obstructs right faith, rather than a single event or discrete sin.

misconceptions.myth: Anantānubandhi passions are so powerful that they make spiritual progress completely impossible for anyone who has ever experienced them.
misconceptions.reality: While anantānubandhi passions are considered extremely harmful and are associated with lower rebirths and obstruction of right faith, Jain teachings also emphasize the possibility of gradual transformation. Through vows, restraint, repentance, and sustained ethical practice, the intensity of passions can be reduced from anantānubandhi to milder forms, allowing for the emergence of right faith and higher spiritual stages. The presence of anantānubandhi passions indicates serious spiritual danger, not an irreversible condition.

misconceptions.myth: Only monks and nuns need to worry about anantānubandhi; laypeople are not affected by such intense passions.
misconceptions.reality: Jain karma theory applies to all souls, lay and monastic alike. Anantānubandhi passions can arise in anyone whose anger, pride, deceit, or greed becomes deeply rooted and repeatedly overrides ethical considerations. Lay practice explicitly includes reflection on and reduction of passions, and many lay-oriented texts warn against anantānubandhi states as much as monastic manuals do.

misconceptions.myth: Anantānubandhi is purely a metaphysical label with no psychological or ethical relevance in daily life.
misconceptions.reality: Although framed in metaphysical terms of karmic bondage and rebirth, anantānubandhi is closely tied to observable psychological patterns: chronic rage, rigid egoism, manipulative deceit, and pervasive greed. Jain teachers use the concept to help practitioners recognize and address these patterns ethically and emotionally, linking inner transformation with the reduction of karmic bondage. Thus, anantānubandhi has direct ethical and psychological relevance, not merely abstract cosmological significance.
